questions.question: Fifteen years ago, the average age of a mother and her daughter was 18 years. After 15 years, the average age of the mother and three times the age of the daughter will be 66 years. What is the difference between their present ages?
questions.questionHtml: Fifteen years ago, the average age of a mother and her daughter was 18 years. After 15 years, the average age of the mother and three times the age of the daughter will be 66 years. What is the difference between their present ages?
questions.solution:
15 years ago average = 18
⇒ Sum then = 36
⇒ Present sum = 36 + 30 = 66

After 15 years:
Average of (Mother + 3 × Daughter) = 66
⇒ Total = 132

So,
(M + 15) + 3(D + 15) = 132
M + 3D = 72

Now,
M + D = 66
M + 3D = 72

Subtract:
2D = 6 ⇒ D = 3

M = 66 − 3 = 63

Difference = 63 − 3 = 60 years

Now substitute:

= 2(52) + 2(46)
= 104 + 92
= 196

questions.solution:
Rohit is 7th from left

Kunal is 10th from right

Suman is 12th from right and is exactly between Rohit and Kunal

From the right end, Kunal is at position 10 and Suman at 12, so there are 2 people between Suman and Kunal

Since Suman is exactly between Rohit and Kunal, the same number of people (2) must be between Rohit and Suman

So Rohit is 2 places left of Suman

Suman from right = 12
Rohit from left = 7

Total people = 7 + 12 + 1 = 20

questions.question: Read the following passage and answer the given questions accordingly: In modern consumerist societies, "freedom" is often equated with "choice." We are bombarded with an array of options for everything—from the brand of toothpaste we use to the career paths we pursue. While having choices is fundamentally better than having none, psychologists have identified a phenomenon known as the "Paradox of Choice." When the number of options exceeds a certain threshold, the cognitive burden of making a decision becomes exhausting. Instead of feeling empowered, the consumer feels anxious and paralyzed. The psychologist Barry Schwartz argues that this abundance of choice leads to two negative outcomes. First, it produces paralysis rather than liberation. With so many options to choose from, people find it difficult to settle on any one choice, often deferring the decision indefinitely. Second, even if we manage to make a choice, we end up less satisfied with the result than we would be if we had fewer options. This is due to "opportunity cost"—the nagging feeling that by choosing 'Option A', we have missed out on the potentially superior 'Option B' or 'C'. This psychological trap is exacerbated by social media, which provides a constant stream of curated highlights from other people's lives. This creates a "comparison culture" where our choices are constantly measured against an idealized version of someone else’s reality. To mitigate the effects of choice overload, experts suggest adopting a "satisficer" mindset rather than a "maximizer" one. A maximizer strives to make the absolute best choice possible, involving exhaustive research and comparison. A satisficer, on the other hand, identifies a set of criteria and chooses the first option that meets those standards, leading to greater long-term contentment and lower stress. questions.question: Read the following passage and answer the given questions accordingly: In modern consumerist societies, "freedom" is often equated with "choice." We are bombarded with an array of options for everything—from the brand of toothpaste we use to the career paths we pursue. While having choices is fundamentally better than having none, psychologists have identified a phenomenon known as the "Paradox of Choice." When the number of options exceeds a certain threshold, the cognitive burden of making a decision becomes exhausting. Instead of feeling empowered, the consumer feels anxious and paralyzed. The psychologist Barry Schwartz argues that this abundance of choice leads to two negative outcomes. First, it produces paralysis rather than liberation. With so many options to choose from, people find it difficult to settle on any one choice, often deferring the decision indefinitely. Second, even if we manage to make a choice, we end up less satisfied with the result than we would be if we had fewer options. This is due to "opportunity cost"—the nagging feeling that by choosing 'Option A', we have missed out on the potentially superior 'Option B' or 'C'. This psychological trap is exacerbated by social media, which provides a constant stream of curated highlights from other people's lives. This creates a "comparison culture" where our choices are constantly measured against an idealized version of someone else’s reality. To mitigate the effects of choice overload, experts suggest adopting a "satisficer" mindset rather than a "maximizer" one. A maximizer strives to make the absolute best choice possible, involving exhaustive research and comparison. A satisficer, on the other hand, identifies a set of criteria and chooses the first option that meets those standards, leading to greater long-term contentment and lower stress.
